payload.title: Disaster Recovery: service-failure resolution sequence

steps.what: STOP. Do not check the provider status page. Do not blame the platform.
steps.why: External errors are rare; self-caused config mutations are common (BLAME-EXTERNAL-1).

steps.what: CHANGE AUDIT: enumerate every change made to the failing zone/account/service in the last 7 days.
steps.why: The most common root cause is a change made by this system minutes/hours/days earlier (CHANGE-AUDIT-FIRST-1).
steps.scope: DNS records, routing rules, firewall rules, worker filters, bindings, deployments, secrets, rate limits, re-registrations.

substeps.why: Deploys and config edits are version-controlled.
Session-level changes may not be committed.
Prior-session actions are the classic silent killer.

steps.what: DIFFERENTIAL PROOF: compare the failing component against a sibling that works.
steps.why: The difference IS the root cause (canonical: 10/11 domains worked; only qnfo.org - the one with DROP rules - failed).
steps.scope: Sibling domains, sibling routes, sibling workers.

steps.what: REVERT/ROLLBACK the suspicious change BEFORE trying anything else.
steps.why: If the service recovers, the change was the cause; document it as an anti-pattern and never re-introduce it.
steps.scope: Rollback = deploy revert, rule delete, config restore.

steps.what: ONLY AFTER steps 1-4 exhaust every local mutation hypothesis: consider external causes.
steps.why: Prevents misdiagnosing self-damage as external failure (the 2026-08-10 email-10002 case was self-inflicted DROP rules, never a platform incident).
steps.scope: External attribution requires a differential test first.

payload.prose: When a service fails, the first diagnostic question is 'What did I change recently?' not 'Is the platform down?'. Execute the sequence in order; each step cites its evidence.
